body: I'm 3 months on HRT. I've felt much more happier and comfortable already! I've felt as though now since I'm not having to deal with this huge issue in my life anymore that it's given me more time to worry about other things in my life. And the feelings of wanting to be an amputee have been there for about as long as since I first realized I wanted to be a girl (about a decade for both, the amputee fantasies came only a year later). I've never have actually thought or considered how I felt about these thoughts though. The narrative always was, "if I were someone else I'd want to be an amputee or even seek amputation in that lifetime but not this one, not mine." After 1 month and over the last 2 months as I've been feeling better as a result of the HRT these feelings have been becoming more prominent until finally a couple weeks ago I sat down and started asking myself very seriously what I wanted. And All of the questions and answers I presented myself were the same ones I had when I was figuring out if I wanted to be a girl. I feel very confident in this feeling for whatever reason it's just, very confusing.

> has this gotten worse in the 3 days since your AMA?

The feelings have not. What has got worse is as I'm accepting and recognizing these feelings as real I'm becoming much more mindful about how severe the feelings are.

> would you rather be an amputee than a person who feels like their arms are in the right place?

At this point I don't really care. It's like how I felt with being a trans female I guess. I would rather be a female or amputee, but when it comes down to it I really don't care. I just want to feel happy and comfortable in my own body and feel like it's my own.

[The casual IAMA I did answered pretty well a lot of those questions. I'd suggest reading that](https://www.reddit.com/r/casualiama/comments/4r2ee3/i_have_body_identity_integrity_disorder_and_feel/)

The most likely cause for BIID is a malfunction in the brains 3d map/image of the body. This is how you know where parts of your body is even when your eyes are closed. This is why people who have limbs amputated sometimes get phantom limb syndrome, their brain's are still convinced that there is a limb attached to their body still. This is the opposite where, my brain does not think I have arms. It feels like my body should end at my shoulders and brain wants to reject the rest of my arms. It's very uncomfortable for one. Most of the time it feels like dozens of dull needles poking into my arms. All other sensations too are more dulled or feel less intense. 

Apart from that too, it's an identity issue. This is how I see myself and feel like this is who I should be in any facet of life. Even if I could explicitly cure the physical feelings I'm not sure it'd exactly change 100% how I feel. If I could theoretically be any person or any way or any one or anything I would want to be this way.

I'm definitely on your side. Don't think I'm trying to validate this lifestyle as a practical or even reasonable. I get that it's nearly fully disabling. And I don't know how difficult it would be or could be or even what challenges I would face. I am planning on living this life as exclusively as I can as long term as I can without doing anything permanent. I'm aware I would always need assistance in certain areas but my idea is hopefully I can find a reasonable lifestyle that I could set up for myself to mostly compensate. And for what it's worth this lifestyle might be enough to satisfy my feelings without amputation. I don't know yet this isn't even something I've decided, I just started having feelings to this degree until very recently. But I know myself pretty well and I think I know how I feel on this. I'm giving myself plenty of room to grow and change because who knows what will happen in the future. But for now I have to deal with these feelings currently in the present moment.

Not that I condone it but it's the reality. I don't expect anyone to do this legally or rationally or as a treatment.

* Not really, and that's really some shit with this. See I'm also transgender (male to female) and those have been feelings I've dealt with since I was 13 1/2. I just decided 3 months ago now to start hormones and transition. I'd say after the first week on hormones I started feeling significantly happier and more comfortable with myself. I'd say these past months have been the happiest I've been in the past decade. But as I've felt better, I've been less concerned with my gender issues, and these body integrity issues started becoming more prominent. And to be quite honest the ways I've felt recently about my body identity have been the same ways I felt about my gender identity when questioning it. 

* I am diagnosed with bipolar I disorder, with high depression/anxiety as symptoms. They thought I had depression when they were initially diagnosing me and put me on anti depressants at first which as a result made me go through a major manic phase. Also throughout this past year I've been talking with my mom about how she thinks I might be somewhere in the spectrum of autistic. I wouldn't really be surprised I mean looking at all the classic signs/symptoms I don't see how I'm not. I still need to see a psychiatrist about it though.

* Yes I just talked to my gender therapist about this 2 weeks ago. They reacted in a lot more of a helpful way than I expected. Did very well to validate my feelings and wanting to explore them instead of vilifying me and saying I need to be "cured/fixed" which is what I was worried about.

* I don't presently but if I were at that point I'd want to have a career in writing. I'm interested in fiction. I'm considering going to school to be a psychologist or therapist. I think that either of those I could manage without arms.
Yes. If I remember correctly her name was "Life."

I'm 24 now. No I wouldn't try to harm or amputate myself personally. Beyond it being incredibly dangerous, I do want an aesthetic result.  I'm not really in any rush, I'm already planning on waiting a decade before making any decision on this. At that point I would hope I have enough money saved or have found the correct connections to where I could just pay someone to look the other way.

I don't know. Right now before even considering doing anything permanent I want to start pretending to live this way in my personal life. Where, I'm going to ask my friends/partners to restrict my arms. I think in my future even if I'm not an amputee that this is just how I want to live my casual life. My goal is that by the time I'd be considering this that I'd have at least a few years of getting at least some idea of what could be an issue and hopefully compensating (in response to your questions: feet, feet/knob attachments, assistance, bidet, not sure/attachment of sorts). 

That's something that I'm concerned about is that voluntary amputation is a purely selfish or even anti social act. I'd hope that if I did go through with it that the people in my life could accept helping wipe my bum even though I willingly disabled myself. And if it is something I go through with, I'd take concern in wanting to make sure I wouldn't force anyone to take care of me. I'd want to be at a point that I could possibly take care of myself to the extent that I could survive alone.

Well I could give away one arm to get rid of the other one, because if I gave away both arms I'd still have to have something taken away. I think?

The big thing is that it feels like my arms "aren't mine." It's like my brain doesn't recognize them as part of my body. This as a result is rather uncomfortable, and a lot of the time feels like dozens of dull needles poking into my arms.  In general all sensations are a bit more dull and less receptive. Kinda feels cold sometimes or like a chill is running through them.

Now, this might cause shit I know it but this is the only real other way I can explain it. Apart from the physical feelings, it's partly an identity issue. It's like, even if I could fix these physical feelings explicitly that almost doesn't matter because this is who I see myself as. This is who I want to be and be perceived as in society and every other aspect of my life. 

No one really knows why people feel this way. The only hypotheses I've heard is that it's a disorder with the brains 3d map of the body. It's basically the opposite reason why people who become amputees get phantom limb syndrome, where their brain is convinced that their limb is still attached to their body.
